catalog_quote: Based on my field data, I argue that there are at present five tones in Buyuan Jino, which can be exemplified as follows (Hayashi forthcoming). (2) a. 55 (High level tone) : high and level. It tends to exhibit vowels that are phonetically shortened. /ja55/ 'weave', /fu55thu55/ 'trousers', /wu55/ 'sell' ... b. 44 (Mid level tone) : lower than 55, though still high. /ja44/ 'sweep' ... c. 31 (Low falling tone) : low. /ja31/ 'take', /fu31/ 'deceive', /wu31/ 'buy' ... d. 35 (Rising tone) : rising. Found in relatively few words. ... e. 53 (High falling tone): falling from the top level. ... [fn. 3] Syllable Structure: (C1)(C2)V1(V2)(V3)(C3)/T ... As demonstrated in (3), the tone value [53] occurs at the end of a 'morphological word'. It seems to be found in grammatical morphemes ... tone_statements.quote: Tonemes: /55, 44, 31, 35, 53/ Syllable Structure: (C1)(C2)V1(V2)(V3)(C3)/T ... There are many examples of nouns that express case through tone alternation (8): ... Note that the first-singular pronoun in (8a) is ŋɔ31, whereas in (8b) it is ŋɔ35. The tonal difference between the two pronouns is the result of syntax. The former is slated as the subject, while the latter is the object. The same tonal alternation pattern can be found in (8c) and (8d). The tonemes of the second-singular pronouns in (8c) and (8d) are different for the same reason. In some cases, oblique noun marking occurs by altering the tone to that in 35

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and locator (Hayashi 2012/2013 sec. 3 pp. 22-24, fn. 3, Table 2; sec. 5 p. 31) are confirmed verbatim in the PDF we hold/text. (2) Deciding source: an open-access specialist tone article (2013) by Norihiko Hayashi, the only linguist with modern field data on Buyuan Jino; it states five tonemes per syllable (four distinctive + positional word-final /53/) and syllable template..(C3)/T, and nowhere describes word stress or accent. Against Glottolog's list: Gai 1986 is an older jianzhi whose Buyuan coverage is a 7-page dialect appendix that Hayashi reviews and rejects; Jiang 2010 is a Youle Jino reference grammar (Hayashi p. 21: Gai 1986 is 'the only previous published work on Buyuan Jino'), so neither outranks the held source for this languoid. sources.note: Fn. 1 gives the phonological inventory with five tonemes /55, 44, 31, 35, 53/ and syllable template ending in /T; sec. 2 reports Gai (1986)'s claim that Buyuan Jino marks objects by tone alternation (31 -> 13); sec. 4.1 documents grammatical tone: subject vs object/oblique pronouns differ only in tone (ŋɔ31 NOM vs ŋɔ35 OBL, nɤ31 vs nɤ35) and some oblique nouns take tone 35 (tsu35 'house'); sec. 4.2 notes the subject clitic =ɛ varies 44 ~ 31. Consistent with the 5-toneme statement listed here; adds case-marking tone alternation not in the catalog prose.

sources.note: KAKEN 20720111 research abstract says the Buyuan field data (c. 2,300 lexical items, 550 sentences) allowed 'preliminary reports on the phonology and the tonal development' to be made, and lists this ICSTLL-43 paper (Lund, 2010-10-17) and 'Notes on Buyuan Jino tones and their development' (2011-02-20) as those reports; no text of the 2010 paper seen; its analysis was published in the known 2012/2013 works (five tonemes 55/44/31/35/53).
